passages.t: Twelve disciples who knew only John's baptism
passages.happening:
While Apollos is in Corinth, Paul travels through the inland regions and comes to Ephesus. There he finds some disciples (verse 1) and asks them, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you became believers?” They answer, “we have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit” (verse 2).

“Into what, then, were you baptized?” Paul asks. “The baptism of John,” they reply (verse 3). Paul explains: “John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance. He told the people to believe in the One coming after him, that is, in Jesus” (verse 4).

On hearing this, they are baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus (verse 5). When Paul lays his hands on them, the Holy Spirit comes on them, and they speak in tongues and prophesy (verse 6). There are about twelve men in all (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Ephesus was the great city of the Roman province of Asia, a busy port with a famous temple. Paul had promised to come back ‘if God is willing’ (18:21), and now he does.

He meets ‘some disciples’, followers who in some way had learned from John the Baptist's movement, like Apollos in the last chapter. They had been baptized with John's baptism, a washing that showed a person was turning from sin and getting ready for the one who was coming. But they had not heard that the one John pointed to had come, died, risen, and poured out the Holy Spirit.

‘We have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit’ probably does not mean they had never heard the words ‘Holy Spirit’. John himself had spoken of one who would baptize with the Spirit. It likely means they had not heard that the Spirit had now been given.

So Paul tells them that John pointed to Jesus. They believe, and they are baptized in Jesus' name. Paul lays his hands on them, and the Spirit comes, with tongues and prophecy, as at Pentecost.

‘About twelve’ may remind a reader of the twelve tribes of Israel and the twelve apostles. Luke does not make anything of it.
passages.ot:
John the Baptist had spoken of what was coming: “I baptize you with water for repentance, but after me will come One more powerful than I” (Matthew 3:11), and “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (Luke 3:16).

The gift of the Spirit with prophecy fulfils the promise of Joel: “I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy” (Joel 2:28). Moses had longed for it: “I wish that all the LORD’s people were prophets” (Numbers 11:29).
passages.hard:
Were these men baptized twice? And is this a pattern for believers today, a second experience of the Spirit after baptism? Christians read this passage in different ways. These views are held by faithful believers, and these notes do not choose between them.

On baptism. These men had received John's baptism, not Christian baptism in the name of Jesus. Most readers therefore do not see this as a believer being baptized again. It is the first time they are baptized into Jesus. Nothing in Acts suggests that Apollos, who also knew only John's baptism (18:25), was baptized again; Luke simply says he was taught more accurately. Readers differ on why.

On the Spirit. Pentecostal and many charismatic Christians read this scene, with Samaria in chapter 8, as showing that believers may receive a baptism in the Spirit, often with tongues, as a distinct experience after they first believe. Many other Christians read the twelve as disciples of John who had not yet put their faith in Jesus, so that their believing, their baptism and their receiving of the Spirit together make one full conversion, not a second stage. Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican Christians also link the laying on of hands here with confirmation.

Acts shows no single fixed order: the Spirit is promised with repentance and baptism at Pentecost (2:38), comes after baptism through the apostles' hands in Samaria (8:14-17), comes before baptism in Cornelius's house (10:44-48), and here comes after baptism with the laying on of hands. The notes on 2:1-4 and 2:37-41 (tongues and baptism), 8:14-17 and 10:44-48 set out these readings more fully. All agree that every believer belongs to Christ by his Spirit, and that the Spirit is God's gift.
passages.asks: These men had followed as far as they had been taught, and Paul did not mock them. He asked a good question and told them the rest. Ask whether there is part of the good news you have never really heard. And ask whether you are patient with people who know only part of it.

passages.t: Two years in the hall of Tyrannus
passages.happening:
Paul goes into the synagogue and speaks boldly there for three months, “arguing persuasively about the kingdom of God” (verse 8). But some stubbornly refuse to believe and publicly speak evil of the Way. So Paul takes the disciples and leaves the synagogue, and holds discussions every day in the lecture hall of Tyrannus (verse 9).

“This continued for two years, so that everyone who lived in the province of Asia, Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord” (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Three months in the synagogue is the longest Acts tells of Paul being welcome in one. When some speak against ‘the Way’, an early name for the followers of Jesus (9:2), he does not fight on. He moves to a lecture hall, a place where teachers gave talks. Tyrannus was probably its owner or a teacher who used it. Luke tells us nothing more about him.

For two years Paul teaches there every day. And the word spreads through the whole province of Asia. Paul did not visit every town himself. Those who heard him carried the message home. The churches in other cities of the province, such as Colossae, may have begun this way; Paul's letter to the Colossians suggests he had not visited them himself (Colossians 2:1).
passages.ot:
Paul ‘argued persuasively about the kingdom of God’, the theme of the prophets. Daniel foresaw a kingdom that God himself would set up, “a kingdom that will never be destroyed” (Daniel 2:44).

And the spread of the word through a whole province fits Isaiah's picture of God's word that does its work: “So My word that proceeds from My mouth will not return to Me empty” (Isaiah 55:11).
passages.asks: Paul taught every day for two years, and the people he taught carried the word to places he never went. Ask what you are passing on, and to whom. Much of the good news has travelled not through famous preachers but through ordinary people telling their neighbours.

passages.happening: “God did extraordinary miracles through the hands of Paul” (verse 11), so that even handkerchiefs and aprons that had touched him were taken to the sick, “and the diseases and evil spirits left them” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
Luke is careful how he puts it. It was God who did the miracles. Paul's hands were the means. The cloths were probably the sweat-rags and work aprons of a man who worked a trade (20:34), taken to people who could not come to him.

Luke calls these miracles ‘extraordinary’: not ordinary, even for Acts. Something like this happened with Peter, whose shadow people hoped would fall on the sick (5:15), and with the woman who touched the edge of Jesus' cloak (Mark 5:27-29). In each case the healing is God's free work. It is not a power stored in cloth.
passages.ot:
The Old Testament has one strange story of the same kind: a dead man thrown into Elisha's tomb who “revived and stood up on his feet” when his body “touched the bones of Elisha” (2 Kings 13:21). God, not the bones, gave life.

And the prophets warned against treating holy things as charms. When Israel took the ark of the covenant into battle, saying “it may go with us to save us” (1 Samuel 4:3), they were defeated. God is not carried about in an object to be used.
passages.hard:
Does this passage support selling blessed objects? Some people today sell ‘anointed’ handkerchiefs, prayer cloths or other objects, and suggest that buying them will bring healing or blessing. Nothing in this passage supports that. Luke says plainly that God did these miracles, and he calls them extraordinary. No one sold anything. Paul worked for his living so that he would not burden anyone (20:33-34). Jesus told his followers, “Freely you have received; freely give” (Matthew 10:8). When a man in Samaria offered money for spiritual power, Peter answered, “May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could buy the gift of God with money” (8:20). God's healing cannot be bought, and anyone who sells it is doing what Peter condemned.

Christians do differ on whether God still heals in unusual ways like this today, and many pray with and for the sick, sometimes with anointing oil as James 5:14 describes. That is prayer, freely given, not a product.
passages.asks: God worked through Paul's work-rags, and no one made a profit from it. Ask whether you have ever treated an object, a ritual or a gift of money as a way to make God do something. And if you are sick and praying for healing, bring that prayer straight to God. You do not need to buy anything.

passages.happening:
Some travelling Jewish exorcists try to use the name of the Lord Jesus over people with evil spirits. They say, “I bind you by Jesus, whom Paul proclaims” (verse 13). Seven sons of Sceva, a Jewish chief priest, are doing this (verse 14).

One of the evil spirits answers them, “Jesus I know, and I know about Paul, but who are you?” (verse 15). Then the man with the spirit leaps on them and overpowers them all, so that they run out of the house naked and wounded (verse 16).

This becomes known to all the Jews and Greeks living in Ephesus. Fear comes on them all, “So the name of the Lord Jesus was held in high honor” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
An exorcist was someone who claimed to drive out evil spirits, often by calling on the names of powerful beings. These men had seen Paul's work and tried to use ‘Jesus, whom Paul proclaims’ as one more powerful name in their spells. They did not know Jesus. They were borrowing a name.

Who was Sceva? Luke calls him ‘a Jewish chief priest’. No high priest of that name is known from Jerusalem. The Greek word can mean a member of one of the leading priestly families, not only the high priest himself, so he may have belonged to such a family. Some think the title was simply one he claimed for himself. Luke does not explain.

The spirit's answer is the turning point. ‘Jesus I know, and I know about Paul, but who are you?’ The name of Jesus is not a magic word that works for anyone who says it. It belongs to those who belong to him.

The story is almost comic, seven men running naked into the street, and it is meant to be memorable. But its end is serious: the people of Ephesus see that the name of Jesus is not a tool to be used, and they honour it.
passages.ot:
The Law forbade such practices, among them anyone who “casts spells” (Deuteronomy 18:11), and the third commandment warned against misusing God's name: “You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain” (Exodus 20:7).

Pharaoh's magicians once tried to match God's signs “by their magic arts” (Exodus 7:11), and in the end they could not.
passages.asks: The sons of Sceva used Jesus' name without knowing him. Ask whether you ever use his name, in prayer, in talk or in public, as a tool for your own ends. The question the spirit asked is worth asking yourself: does Jesus know you?

passages.happening: Many who had believed now come forward, confessing and disclosing their deeds (verse 18). A number of those who had practised magic bring their books and burn them in front of everyone. When the value of the books is added up, “the total came to fifty thousand drachmas” (verse 19). “So the word of the Lord powerfully continued to spread and prevail” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Ephesus was known for magic. Ancient writers speak of ‘Ephesian letters’, a set of strange words thought to give protection, which people wrote down and used as charms. People bought written spells for health, love, protection or to harm an enemy.

These are people who ‘had believed’. Their faith had not yet reached every corner of their lives. Now it does. They confess, out loud, what they had been doing. And they do not sell their books to someone else. They burn them, so no one else can use them.

The value was ‘fifty thousand drachmas’. A drachma was a silver coin worth about the same as a Roman denarius, and a denarius was a day's pay for a labourer (Matthew 20:2). Luke gives the figure to show the cost. It was a fortune, given up in public.
passages.ot: The Law told Israel to destroy the objects of false worship, not to profit from them: “You must burn up the images of their gods; do not covet the silver and gold that is on them or take it for yourselves” (Deuteronomy 7:25). When Josiah turned the nation back to God, he cleared out “the mediums and spiritists” and their idols (2 Kings 23:24).
passages.asks: Believers in Ephesus burned their magic books, at great cost, instead of selling them. Ask what you still keep that belongs to your old life: something you use to control your fears or your future without God. Ask what it would cost to give it up, and what it costs to keep it.

passages.happening:
Paul decides, in the Spirit, to go through Macedonia and Achaia and then on to Jerusalem. “After I have been there,” he says, “I must see Rome as well” (verse 21). He sends Timothy and Erastus ahead to Macedonia and stays a while longer in Asia (verse 22).

About that time a great disturbance arises about the Way (verse 23). It begins with a silversmith named Demetrius, who makes silver shrines of Artemis and brings much business to the craftsmen (verse 24). He gathers them and the workmen in related trades: “you know that this business is our source of prosperity” (verse 25). Paul has persuaded a great number of people, in Ephesus and nearly all of Asia, to turn away. “He says that man-made gods are no gods at all” (verse 26). There is danger, he says, not only that their trade will lose its good name, but that the temple of the great goddess Artemis will be discredited, and she will lose her greatness (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
Verse 21 is a hinge in the book. Paul sets his face toward Jerusalem, and then Rome. The rest of Acts follows that road.

Artemis was worshipped in many Greek cities, but the Artemis of Ephesus was the city's own great goddess. Her temple at Ephesus was counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world. An earlier temple had burned in 356 BC and been rebuilt. Her ancient image was covered with rounded shapes whose meaning scholars still debate. The city believed this image had fallen from heaven (verse 35).

Demetrius made ‘silver shrines of Artemis’, small models of her shrine or image, sold to worshippers and visitors. He is honest about what worries him. He starts with money, ‘our source of prosperity’, and then adds the goddess. And he reports Paul's teaching fairly: ‘man-made gods are no gods at all’. That is exactly what Paul taught.

Notice that Luke tells this without sneering at the city. Demetrius and his fellow workers were proud of their goddess and their city, and afraid for their livelihoods. Luke lets them speak in their own words. Their fear was real: the good news was changing what people bought, because it was changing what they worshipped.
passages.ot: The prophets had said what Paul said: “Their idols are silver and gold, made by the hands of men” (Psalm 115:4). Jeremiah mocked the craftsman's idol, which “is shaped with a chisel by the hands of a craftsman” and must be fastened down “so that it will not totter” (Jeremiah 10:3-4). Isaiah described a man who makes a god from what is left of his firewood and prays to it, “Save me, for you are my god” (Isaiah 44:17).
passages.asks: Demetrius cared most about his income, and then about his goddess. Ask what you would defend most fiercely if it were threatened: your faith, or your finances. And notice that when people truly turned to God in Ephesus, their spending changed. Ask whether your faith has reached your money.

passages.happening:
When the men hear this, they are furious and begin shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians” (verse 28). Soon the whole city is in confusion. They rush together into the theatre, dragging Gaius and Aristarchus, Paul's travelling companions from Macedonia (verse 29).

Paul wants to go in to the crowd, but the disciples will not let him (verse 30). Even some officials of the province of Asia, who are his friends, send word begging him not to go into the theatre (verse 31). The assembly is in uproar; some shout one thing and some another, “and most of them did not even know why they were there” (verse 32).

The Jews in the crowd push a man named Alexander forward, and he motions for silence to make a defence (verse 33). But when they realize he is a Jew, they all shout together for about two hours, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
The theatre at Ephesus, cut into the side of a hill, held something over twenty thousand people by most modern estimates. Its ruins can still be seen. It was the place where the people of the city gathered.

Luke tells the scene with a touch of humour. A crowd fills the theatre, shouting, and ‘most of them did not even know why they were there’.

Paul wants to go in. His friends stop him, among them some ‘officials of the province of Asia’, in Greek Asiarchs. These were wealthy, leading men of the province, known from many inscriptions, who were linked with its council and its public festivals. Their exact duties are still debated. That such men were Paul's friends shows how far his message had reached.

‘The Jews in the crowd’ means the Jews of Ephesus who were present that day. They push Alexander forward, probably so that he can explain that the Jewish community had nothing to do with Paul. Jews also refused to worship idols, and they may have feared the riot would turn on them. And it does: as soon as the crowd sees he is a Jew, they shout him down for two hours. This is not Luke speaking against the Jewish people. It is a crowd in a pagan city turning on a Jew for being a Jew. The note on Acts 2:22-28 sets out how this site reads Luke's ‘the Jews’.
passages.ot:
The crowd's chant has the ring of Babylon's boast in Isaiah, and Isaiah's answer: “Bel crouches; Nebo cowers. Their idols weigh down beasts and cattle” (Isaiah 46:1). The gods that a city carries cannot carry the city.

The Psalms describe the same uproar of nations against God: “Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?” (Psalm 2:1).
passages.asks: A crowd shouted for two hours, and most of them did not know why they were there. Ask whether you have ever been swept along by a crowd, online or in person, without knowing what it was about. And notice Paul's friends, who held him back from danger. Ask whether you listen when wise friends tell you not to go.

passages.t: The town clerk calms the city
passages.happening:
At last the city clerk quiets the crowd. “Men of Ephesus,” he says, everyone knows that Ephesus is the guardian of the temple of the great Artemis and of her image, which fell from heaven (verse 35). Since that cannot be denied, “you ought to be calm and not do anything rash” (verse 36).

These men, he says, “have neither robbed our temple nor blasphemed our goddess” (verse 37). If Demetrius and the craftsmen have a complaint, the courts are open and there are proconsuls; let them bring charges there (verse 38). Anything more must be settled in the lawful assembly (verse 39). “For we are in jeopardy of being charged with rioting for today’s events” (verse 40). And he dismisses the assembly (verse 41).
passages.hearers:
The city clerk was a senior official of Ephesus, who dealt with the city's assembly and its records. He was not a Christian, and he does not pretend to be. He is proud of his city's goddess. But he is fair.

He makes four points. Ephesus's honour as ‘guardian of the temple’ is not in danger, so calm down. These men have not robbed the temple or insulted the goddess. If anyone has a real complaint, there are courts and governors. And this riot could get the city into trouble with Rome, which did not like disorder in its cities.

Luke lets a pagan official say what Luke wants his readers to know: the followers of Jesus were not criminals. They had not attacked the temple or mocked the goddess. They had simply taught that man-made gods are not gods, and people had believed it. The clerk, like Gallio in Corinth, finds no crime.

Notice too what Paul's friends did not do. They did not insult Artemis. The city is shown without contempt, its people loyal to their goddess, its officials keeping order. The good news was changing Ephesus from within, by persuasion, not by mockery.
passages.ot:
God can bring order through officials who do not know him. Jeremiah told the exiles in Babylon, “Seek the prosperity of the city to which I have sent you as exiles. Pray to the LORD on its behalf, for if it prospers, you too will prosper” (Jeremiah 29:7). The believers in Ephesus lived as good neighbours in a pagan city, and its own clerk defended them.

And Proverbs commends the calm voice that ends a quarrel: “A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1).
passages.asks: The believers in Ephesus had not robbed temples or mocked the goddess, and even a pagan official could say so. Ask whether your neighbours could say the same of you: that you hold your faith firmly and still treat what they love with respect. And ask whether you speak about other people's beliefs in a way that persuades, or only in a way that wounds.
